sections.title: Study 1 – The Divine Origin and Apostolic Validation of Paul’s Gospel
sections.html:
Passage: Galatians 1:1 – 2:10
Theme: The Divine Origin and Apostolic Validation of Paul’s Gospel

Scripture Focus (ESV)

In Galatians 1:1–2:10 Paul defends the divine origin, content, and authority of the gospel he preaches. This section establishes that the gospel Paul proclaims comes by revelation from God, not from human tradition, and that it was subsequently recognized—though not corrected—by the Jerusalem apostles.

Argument Flow

  1. Divine commissioning and gospel source (1:1–5)
  2. The exclusivity of the true gospel (1:6–10)
  3. Revelation, not human transmission (1:11–17)
  4. Limited contact with Jerusalem leaders (1:18–24)
  5. Apostolic recognition without gospel modification (2:1–10)

Commentary Integration

Douglas J. Moo (BECNT)

Moo stresses that Paul’s defence of his apostleship is inseparable from his defence of the gospel itself. To undermine Paul’s authority is to undermine the gospel’s divine origin. Moo notes that Paul’s delay in consulting Jerusalem demonstrates that the content of his gospel was fixed prior to any apostolic interaction. The Jerusalem meeting in 2:1–10 functions not as an approval hearing but as public confirmation that Gentiles are incorporated into God’s people apart from the Mosaic law.

Moo highlights Titus as a living test case: his uncircumcision confirms that justification by faith alone is not merely theoretical but practically enforced. Any concession on this point would have compromised the truth of the gospel.

Thomas R. Schreiner (ZECNT)

Schreiner emphasizes the revelatory nature of Paul’s gospel. Paul did not receive it from tradition, catechesis, or apostolic chain, but directly from the risen Christ. Schreiner notes that Galatians opens with theological urgency because eternal destinies are at stake—there is no neutral ground between the true gospel and a distorted one.

Regarding the Jerusalem visit, Schreiner argues that apostolic unity rests on shared gospel truth, not hierarchy. James, Peter, and John add nothing to Paul’s message, demonstrating that justification by faith was already the common apostolic confession.

John G. Reisinger (Studies in Galatians)

Reisinger underscores that Galatians dismantles any attempt to place believers back under Mosaic authority. For Reisinger, Paul’s strongest concern is not Jewish custom but the conscience of the believer. Allowing circumcision as a requirement would reinstall Moses as covenant lord over the conscience, nullifying the finished work of Christ.

Reisinger argues that Paul’s resistance to false brothers in 2:4–5 is absolute because freedom of conscience is at stake. The gospel does not merely forgive sins; it liberates the believer from law as covenantal master.

R. L. Solberg (The Law, the Christ, the Promise)

Solberg frames this section as a pastoral defence of the gospel against legalistic corruption. Paul’s language of curse (1:8–9) is not rhetorical excess but a necessary safeguard of grace. To add law-keeping to faith is to exchange Christ’s sufficiency for human effort.

Solberg emphasizes that the Jerusalem apostles recognize distinct missions—Jewish and Gentile—without distinct gospels. The same promise fulfilled in Christ governs both, confirming that the law never functioned as a means of justification.

Theological Synthesis

Together, the commentators agree that Galatians 1:1–2:10 establishes an unalterable gospel grounded in divine revelation, confirmed by apostolic unity, and protected from legalistic intrusion. The law is neither saviour nor covenant authority over believers; Christ alone occupies that role. Apostolic authority serves the gospel—it does not define it.

Key Doctrinal Conclusions

  • The gospel originates in God’s revelation, not human tradition.
  • Any alteration of the gospel places one under divine judgment.
  • Justification by faith alone is assumed as settled apostolic truth.
  • The Mosaic law has no covenantal authority over Gentile believers.
  • Christian unity is grounded in shared gospel truth, not institutional control.

Discussion Questions

  1. Why does Paul pronounce a curse on anyone preaching another gospel?
  2. How does Paul’s conversion and calling challenge ideas of apostolic succession?
  3. Why is Titus’s uncircumcision theologically decisive in this section?
  4. What does this passage teach about unity and diversity within the church?
  5. How do modern forms of legalism parallel the problem Paul addresses in Galatia?

sections.title: Study 2 – Justification by Faith Alone — The Antioch Confrontation
sections.html:
Passage: Galatians 2:11 – 2:21
Theme: Justification by Faith Alone — The Antioch Confrontation

Scripture Focus (ESV)

Galatians 2:11–21 records Paul’s public confrontation with Peter at Antioch and provides the clearest and most concentrated statement of justification by faith in the letter. Here narrative becomes doctrine: Peter’s withdrawal from Gentiles is not a social misstep but a denial of the truth of the gospel.

Argument Flow

  1. Peter’s withdrawal and hypocrisy (2:11–13)
  2. The public rebuke grounded in gospel truth (2:14)
  3. Jews and Gentiles justified the same way (2:15–16)
  4. Law does not justify but condemns (2:17–18)
  5. Union with Christ: death to law, life to God (2:19–21)

Commentary Integration

Douglas J. Moo (BECNT)

Moo identifies this passage as the theological heart of Galatians. Peter’s behaviour implies that observance of the law is necessary for full covenant membership, which contradicts the gospel Paul preaches. Moo stresses that justification by faith is not a secondary doctrine but the very definition of the gospel. To add law-works as a condition for table fellowship is to rebuild what Christ has torn down.

Moo notes that Paul’s rebuke is public because the sin was public and because the truth of the gospel was at stake. The phrase ‘not acting in line with the truth of the gospel’ (2:14) shows that behaviour can deny doctrine even when words appear orthodox.

Thomas R. Schreiner (ZECNT)

Schreiner emphasizes that justification by faith apart from works of the law is stated three times in verse 16 for rhetorical force. Paul leaves no room for a blended system. The law reveals sin but cannot justify sinners. Schreiner argues that Peter’s withdrawal functionally placed Gentiles under the Mosaic law, contradicting the grace of Christ.

Schreiner highlights verse 19 as crucial: believers have died to the law through the law. The law pronounces death, and in Christ that death has been fully executed. As a result, the believer now lives to God apart from the law’s jurisdiction.

John G. Reisinger (Studies in Galatians)

Reisinger treats this passage as decisive for the role of the law in the believer’s conscience. To return to law-keeping as a means of maintaining fellowship is to deny union with Christ. Reisinger stresses that justification by faith is not merely an entry doctrine but the governing principle of the Christian life.

For Reisinger, ‘I have been crucified with Christ’ (2:20) means the law has lost all authority to accuse, condemn, or govern the believer’s conscience. Sanctification flows from union with Christ, not from renewed submission to Moses.

R. L. Solberg (The Law, the Christ, the Promise)

Solberg frames the Antioch incident pastorally and polemically. Peter’s fear of the circumcision party demonstrates how easily even apostles can drift when social pressure replaces gospel conviction. Paul’s rebuke protects Gentile believers from being treated as second-class Christians.

Solberg emphasizes that justification by faith alone levels the ground entirely. If righteousness could be gained through the law, then ‘Christ died for nothing’ (2:21). This verse exposes every form of legalism as an implicit denial of the cross.

Theological Synthesis

Galatians 2:11–21 establishes justification by faith alone as the controlling truth of the Christian life. Law observance cannot add to Christ’s work, secure fellowship, or restrain sin. Union with Christ redefines righteousness, identity, and obedience. To return to the law is to rebuild what God has destroyed.

Key Doctrinal Conclusions

  • Justification by faith alone is essential, not peripheral.
  • Law-keeping cannot secure righteousness or fellowship.
  • Christian behaviour must align with gospel truth.
  • Union with Christ governs both justification and sanctification.
  • Any system adding law to grace nullifies the cross.

Discussion Questions

  1. Why does Paul confront Peter publicly rather than privately?
  2. How can behaviour deny the gospel even when doctrine is verbally affirmed?
  3. Why does Paul repeat justification by faith three times in verse 16?
  4. What does it mean to be ‘crucified with Christ’ in daily Christian life?
  5. Where do modern churches subtly rebuild what Christ has torn down?

sections.title: Study 3 – Faith, the Spirit, and Redemption from the Curse
sections.html:
Passage: Galatians 3:1 – 3:14
Theme: Faith, the Spirit, and Redemption from the Curse

Scripture Focus (ESV)

In Galatians 3:1–14 Paul turns from narrative to direct theological argument. He appeals to the Galatians’ own experience of receiving the Spirit, to Abraham’s justification by faith, and to Christ’s redemptive death to demonstrate that righteousness comes by faith alone and not by works of the law. To return to the law is not spiritual progress but regression into curse.

Argument Flow

  1. Rebuke for abandoning the Spirit for the flesh (3:1–5)
  2. Abraham justified by faith (3:6–9)
  3. The law brings curse, not blessing (3:10–12)
  4. Christ redeems from the curse by becoming a curse (3:13–14)

Commentary Integration

Douglas J. Moo (BECNT)

Moo notes that Paul begins with sharp rebuke because the Galatians’ error is irrational and spiritually dangerous. They received the Spirit not by works of the law but by hearing with faith. For Moo, the Spirit is the clearest evidence that the new age has arrived and that justification is already settled.

Moo emphasizes that Abraham’s justification by faith establishes a pattern fulfilled, not overturned, by the gospel. Those who belong to Christ inherit Abraham’s blessing without submitting to the Mosaic law.

Thomas R. Schreiner (ZECNT)

Schreiner stresses the salvation-historical contrast between promise and law. The law was never intended to provide life; its function was to reveal sin and pronounce curse. Anyone who relies on the law places themselves under its demand for perfect obedience.

Schreiner highlights the representative nature of Christ’s death. By becoming a curse for us, Christ exhausts the law’s condemning power, so that the blessing of Abraham and the promised Spirit come to believers by faith.

John G. Reisinger (Studies in Galatians)

Reisinger sees this passage as devastating to any attempt to use the law as a means of sanctification. The Spirit who began the Christian life must also carry it forward. Trying to perfect oneself by the flesh is to deny the sufficiency of Christ and the Spirit.

Reisinger underscores that the law cannot bless a sinner and cannot sanctify a believer. Its only covenantal function is to curse. Christ alone secures blessing and life.

R. L. Solberg (The Law, the Christ, the Promise)

Solberg emphasizes Paul’s appeal to experience: the Galatians know how they received the Spirit. Their lived experience confirms the gospel of grace. The Judaizers’ message asks believers to abandon faith for effort.

Solberg highlights that Christ becoming a curse is central to Paul’s argument. The law’s curse is not mitigated but fully borne by Christ. This leaves no remaining curse for those who are in Him.

Theological Synthesis

Galatians 3:1–14 establishes that the Spirit, not the law, governs the Christian life. Abraham’s faith anticipates the gospel, the law intensifies curse, and Christ removes it entirely. To seek righteousness through law is to abandon both the Spirit and the cross.

Key Doctrinal Conclusions

  • The Christian life begins and continues by faith.
  • The Spirit is received through faith, not law-keeping.
  • The law exposes sin and pronounces curse but cannot give life.
  • Christ fully bears the law’s curse on behalf of His people.
  • Returning to the law is spiritual regression, not maturity.

Discussion Questions

  1. Why does Paul appeal to the Galatians’ experience of the Spirit?
  2. How does Abraham function as a model for justification by faith?
  3. Why does Paul say all who rely on the law are under a curse?
  4. What does it mean that Christ became a curse for us?
  5. How do modern believers attempt to be ‘perfected by the flesh’ today?

sections.title: Study 4 – Promise, Law, Heirs, and Sonship
sections.html:
Passage: Galatians 3:15 – 4:7
Theme: Promise, Law, Heirs, and Sonship

Scripture Focus (ESV)

In Galatians 3:15–4:7 Paul advances his argument by contrasting the permanence of God’s promise with the temporary, subordinate role of the Mosaic law. The promise given to Abraham finds its fulfillment in Christ, resulting in believers becoming heirs and sons who receive the Spirit. The law functioned as a guardian until Christ came, but it no longer defines the believer’s covenantal status.

Argument Flow

  1. The inviolability of God’s promise (3:15–18)
  2. The purpose and limitation of the law (3:19–22)
  3. The law as guardian until Christ (3:23–25)
  4. Sonship and unity in Christ (3:26–29)
  5. Heirs liberated from guardianship (4:1–7)

Commentary Integration

Douglas J. Moo (BECNT)

Moo emphasizes that Paul’s analogy of a human covenant underscores the unchangeable nature of God’s promise. The Mosaic law, given later, cannot annul or modify the promise made to Abraham. For Moo, the law’s role was never salvific but custodial, exposing sin and preserving Israel until Christ.

Moo notes that the ‘guardian’ metaphor highlights both the authority and the temporariness of the law. Once faith has come, believers are no longer under this guardian but have entered full sonship in Christ.

Thomas R. Schreiner (ZECNT)

Schreiner stresses the salvation-historical logic of the passage. The law was added because of transgressions, not to provide life or righteousness. Its function was to imprison everything under sin so that the promise might be received by faith.

Schreiner highlights that sonship marks a decisive shift in redemptive history. Believers are no longer minors under supervision but mature heirs who cry ‘Abba, Father’ through the indwelling Spirit.

John G. Reisinger (Studies in Galatians)

Reisinger sees this passage as pivotal for understanding covenantal transition. The law belonged to a previous covenantal administration and has no authority over those in Christ. Believers are sons, not servants, and relate to God directly through Christ, not through Moses.

Reisinger emphasizes that returning to the law is a regression from sonship to slavery. The Spirit’s presence testifies that the believer’s status has fundamentally changed.

R. L. Solberg (The Law, the Christ, the Promise)

Solberg frames Paul’s argument around the supremacy of promise over law. The inheritance comes by promise, not performance. The law served a temporary, preparatory role that ended with the arrival of Christ.

Solberg highlights the pastoral force of Paul’s argument: to submit again to the law is to deny one’s identity as a son and heir. The Spirit’s cry of ‘Abba’ confirms relational intimacy, not legal probation.

Theological Synthesis

Galatians 3:15–4:7 teaches that God’s promise governs salvation history. The law functioned temporarily to restrain and expose sin, but it was never intended to define righteousness. In Christ, believers are heirs and sons who enjoy direct access to God through the Spirit.

Key Doctrinal Conclusions

  • God’s promise cannot be annulled by later law.
  • The Mosaic law was temporary and subordinate.
  • Justification and inheritance come through faith in Christ.
  • Believers are sons and heirs, not slaves or minors.
  • The Spirit confirms adoption and new covenant status.

Discussion Questions

  1. Why does Paul stress the permanence of God’s promise?
  2. What does it mean that the law was ‘added because of transgressions’?
  3. How does the guardian metaphor clarify the role of the law?
  4. Why is sonship central to Paul’s argument?
  5. How do believers today struggle to live as sons rather than slaves?

sections.title: Study 5 – Regression, Pastoral Appeal, and the Two Covenants
sections.html:
Passage: Galatians 4:8 – 4:31
Theme: Regression, Pastoral Appeal, and the Two Covenants

Scripture Focus (ESV)

In Galatians 4:8–31 Paul turns from theological exposition to urgent pastoral appeal. He warns the Galatians that returning to the law is a return to slavery, pleads with them on the basis of their former relationship with him, and finally delivers a scriptural verdict using the account of Hagar and Sarah. The issue is not ethnic identity but covenantal status.

Argument Flow

  1. Returning to slavery under weak and beggarly elements (4:8–11)
  2. Paul’s personal appeal and pastoral concern (4:12–20)
  3. The allegory of Hagar and Sarah: two covenants (4:21–31)

Commentary Integration

Douglas J. Moo (BECNT)

Moo emphasizes that Paul’s concern in this passage is not theoretical but relational. The Galatians’ movement toward law-observance represents a real regression from freedom to slavery. Moo notes that the ‘elemental principles’ refer to basic religious systems that enslave, whether pagan or Jewish, when they function apart from Christ.

Regarding the Hagar–Sarah allegory, Moo stresses that Paul is not allegorizing at will but drawing covenantal implications from redemptive history. The contrast is between promise and flesh, freedom and slavery.

Thomas R. Schreiner (ZECNT)

Schreiner highlights the seriousness of observing ‘days, months, seasons, and years’ as a return to bondage. What began as a gracious calling is being exchanged for legal obligation. Paul’s fear is not exaggerated; the gospel itself is at stake.

Schreiner explains that the two women represent two covenants: one producing slaves, the other free children. The contrast is absolute. To align with Sinai is to forfeit freedom in Christ.

John G. Reisinger (Studies in Galatians)

Reisinger argues that Galatians 4 demolishes the idea that the Mosaic covenant continues as a rule of life for believers. Returning to law observance is equated with returning to pagan bondage because both place the believer under principles that cannot give life.

Reisinger sees the Hagar–Sarah contrast as decisive: the old covenant produces slaves; the new covenant produces sons. There is no middle category and no gradual transition.

R. L. Solberg (The Law, the Christ, the Promise)

Solberg emphasizes the pastoral tone of Paul’s appeal. Paul is not winning an argument but pleading for the spiritual safety of his converts. Legalism always masquerades as devotion but ultimately destroys assurance.

Solberg highlights that Paul’s use of Genesis underscores continuity of promise without continuity of covenantal obligation. The children of promise are defined by faith, not by adherence to Sinai.

Theological Synthesis

Galatians 4:8–31 presents a stark choice between slavery and freedom. Paul’s pastoral anguish flows from covenantal clarity: believers belong to the covenant of promise, not the covenant of law. To return to the law is to deny one’s identity as a child of the free woman.

Key Doctrinal Conclusions

  • Returning to the law is a return to slavery.
  • Legalism and paganism share the same enslaving structure.
  • The Mosaic covenant produces bondage, not sonship.
  • The new covenant produces free children through promise.
  • Christian identity must be guarded against religious regression.

Discussion Questions

  1. Why does Paul equate returning to the law with returning to pagan slavery?
  2. What makes legalism spiritually dangerous even when it appears devout?
  3. How does Paul’s personal appeal strengthen his theological argument?
  4. Why does Paul frame Hagar and Sarah in terms of two covenants?
  5. Where do modern believers face pressure to choose slavery over freedom?

sections.title: Study 6 – Freedom in Christ and Life by the Spirit
sections.html:
Passage: Galatians 5:1 – 5:26
Theme: Freedom in Christ and Life by the Spirit

Scripture Focus (ESV)

In Galatians 5:1–26 Paul turns to the lived outworking of gospel freedom. Christian liberty is not license, nor is it law-keeping, but Spirit-led life flowing from union with Christ. Freedom is guarded against legalism on the one hand and fleshly indulgence on the other.

Argument Flow

  1. Christ has set us free — do not submit again to slavery (5:1–6)
  2. Law-keeping severs one from Christ (5:7–12)
  3. Freedom expressed through love, not flesh (5:13–15)
  4. Walking by the Spirit versus gratifying the flesh (5:16–18)
  5. Works of the flesh contrasted with fruit of the Spirit (5:19–26)

Commentary Integration

Douglas J. Moo (BECNT)

Moo emphasizes that Christian freedom is the controlling theme of the chapter. Circumcision is not a neutral practice but a covenantal commitment that obligates one to the whole law. To accept circumcision is to abandon Christ as the sole basis of righteousness.

Moo notes that life by the Spirit is not lawlessness. The Spirit produces love, which fulfills the moral intent of the law without placing believers under its authority.

Thomas R. Schreiner (ZECNT)

Schreiner stresses that freedom from the law does not result in moral chaos. The Spirit opposes the flesh, producing real ethical transformation. Believers are not under law precisely because they are led by the Spirit.

Schreiner highlights that the works of the flesh represent life dominated by sin, while the fruit of the Spirit reflects the new creation life inaugurated in Christ.

John G. Reisinger (Studies in Galatians)

Reisinger argues that sanctification must be understood through the same gospel that justifies. Returning to law as a rule of life undermines freedom and assurance. The Spirit, not the law, restrains the flesh and produces holiness.

Reisinger emphasizes that ‘law of Christ’ language cannot be equated with the Mosaic code. Obedience flows from relationship, not covenantal obligation.

R. L. Solberg (The Law, the Christ, the Promise)

Solberg highlights Paul’s pastoral balance. Freedom is protected from both legalism and libertinism. The Spirit empowers love, which expresses true freedom.

Solberg stresses that the flesh–Spirit conflict is not resolved by rules but by reliance on the Spirit given through Christ.

Theological Synthesis

Galatians 5:1–26 teaches that freedom in Christ is Spirit-governed life. The law neither secures righteousness nor produces holiness. Walking by the Spirit fulfills God’s intent without returning to slavery.

Key Doctrinal Conclusions

  • Christ sets believers free from the law as covenant.
  • Legalism severs reliance on Christ.
  • Freedom is expressed through love.
  • The Spirit, not the law, produces holiness.
  • The fruit of the Spirit marks new covenant life.

Discussion Questions

  1. Why does Paul link circumcision with slavery rather than obedience?
  2. How does walking by the Spirit protect against both legalism and license?
  3. What distinguishes works of the flesh from fruit of the Spirit?
  4. Why does Paul say believers are not under law if led by the Spirit?
  5. How can freedom be misunderstood in the Christian life?

sections.title: Study 7 – New Creation Life, Community, and the Final Verdict
sections.html:
Passage: Galatians 6:1 – 6:18
Theme: New Creation Life, Community, and the Final Verdict

Scripture Focus (ESV)

In Galatians 6:1–18 Paul concludes the letter by applying gospel freedom to life in the Christian community and by issuing a final, unmistakable verdict against legalism. The Christian life is marked by mutual care, Spirit-shaped responsibility, perseverance in doing good, and boasting only in the cross of Christ. The controlling reality is not law observance but the new creation.

Argument Flow

  1. Restoring the fallen and bearing burdens (6:1–5)
  2. Shared responsibility in teaching and generosity (6:6)
  3. Sowing and reaping according to the Spirit (6:7–10)
  4. Paul’s final warning against the circumcision party (6:11–13)
  5. Boasting only in the cross and the rule of the new creation (6:14–18)

Commentary Integration

Douglas J. Moo (BECNT)

Moo emphasizes that Paul’s ethical instructions flow directly from the gospel rather than from law observance. Bearing one another’s burdens fulfills the ‘law of Christ,’ which Moo understands as Christ’s self-giving love rather than a reintroduction of the Mosaic law.

Moo notes that Paul’s reference to large letters signals the seriousness of his closing argument. The circumcision advocates boast in visible markers, while Paul boasts only in the cross, which marks the end of the old order.

Thomas R. Schreiner (ZECNT)

Schreiner highlights the communal nature of Spirit-led life. Restoration, burden-bearing, and perseverance in doing good are evidence of the new creation. These exhortations do not contradict justification by faith but demonstrate its fruit.

Schreiner stresses that the cross redefines the world entirely. Believers are crucified to the world, and the world to them. The decisive category is not circumcision but new creation.

John G. Reisinger (Studies in Galatians)

Reisinger argues that Galatians 6 confirms the complete removal of the Mosaic covenant from the believer’s life. Ethics arise from life in Christ, not from tablets of stone. The ‘law of Christ’ reflects relational obedience empowered by the Spirit.

Reisinger underscores that boasting in the cross excludes all human merit. Any system that reintroduces law as covenant authority undermines the finality of Christ’s work.

R. L. Solberg (The Law, the Christ, the Promise)

Solberg frames Paul’s conclusion as both pastoral and polemical. Paul exposes the circumcision party’s motives: they seek external conformity to avoid persecution. True allegiance to Christ embraces the offense of the cross.

Solberg emphasizes that the new creation functions as Paul’s final rule. Identity, assurance, and ethics flow from what God has done in Christ, not from adherence to a covenant that has passed.

Theological Synthesis

Galatians 6:1–18 presents the lived reality of gospel freedom. The community shaped by the Spirit bears burdens, restores gently, perseveres in good, and boasts only in the cross. The letter closes by anchoring everything in the new creation, which renders circumcision and uncircumcision irrelevant.

Key Doctrinal Conclusions

  • Gospel freedom produces communal responsibility.
  • The ‘law of Christ’ reflects Spirit-empowered love, not Mosaic obligation.
  • Sowing to the Spirit leads to eternal life.
  • The cross ends boasting in human effort.
  • The new creation is the final governing reality.

Discussion Questions

  1. How does burden-bearing fulfill the ‘law of Christ’?
  2. Why does Paul warn against boasting in religious markers?
  3. How does sowing and reaping apply to daily Christian life?
  4. What does it mean to be a new creation?
  5. How does boasting only in the cross shape Christian identity and community?
